The old caption's "over registers", which said what the instruction set's states are, is gone. So the reader re-reads, unsure which layer is the state machine or what its states are.

problem: p1 and p2 set up the keystroke as Enter after typing google.com, which loads a page. The figure (GET /search, index lookup, results ranked) and the caption ("One search") follow a search query instead, and with nothing typed but an address the reader cannot tell what is searched or whose JavaScript "builds the request". The strip's "A first visit" note (later searches skip DNS, TCP, TLS) makes it harder to fit a page load and a search into one Enter.

Leave p1 (the interview question) and the figure title as they are.

quote: what happens when you type google.com into your browser and press Enter?
problem: The question in p1 and the path in the figure describe two different keystrokes. When you type google.com in the address bar, the browser's own navigation code (C++, not page JavaScript) asks www.google.com for GET /. No page JavaScript is running yet, and there is no /search, index lookup or ranking. The figure instead has JavaScript build GET /search, which can only happen on a Google page that has already loaded. That page's connection is normally still open, so DNS, TCP and TLS are skipped, as the figure's own strip says of later searches. So the strip's label "A first visit" contradicts the JS station, and the reader comes away thinking that typing google.com makes JavaScript send a search.
fix: In p2, say which keystroke is traced: "The trace below follows the question's sibling, a search typed into Google's page, from the moment your finger closes a contact...". In the strip, replace the third bullet's opening with: "*A cold start.* The trace assumes the page's connection and DNS entry have expired; a search made while they are fresh skips DNS, TCP and TLS; and once a browser has learned Google speaks QUIC, ..."
reason: Real mismatch. The headline question is 'type google.com and press Enter' (the browser itself requests GET /), but the figure traces page JavaScript building GET /search, which only happens on an already loaded Google page. The strip's 'A first visit' then contradicts the JS station, because a loaded page's connection is normally still open. A reader who knows the omnibox behaviour will stop here. Fix the framing, not the drawing.
judge_fix: p2: replace 'follows that keystroke from the moment your finger closes a contact on a key' with 'follows the nearest case that touches every layer, a search typed into Google's own page and sent with Enter, from the moment your finger closes a contact on a key'. Strip, third bullet: '*A cold start.* The trace assumes the page has sat idle, so its connection has closed and its DNS answer has expired. A search made while they are fresh skips DNS, TCP and TLS; and once a browser has learned Google speaks QUIC, the request rides UDP where TCP is drawn here (Fig 10.9).'

quote: V8's event loop picks it up (12)
problem: V8 has no event loop; the program that embeds it supplies one. In Chrome, Blink runs the HTML event loop on the renderer's main thread (HTML Standard §8.1.7: "user agents must use event loops"). In Node it is libuv, as the book's own Fig 12.6 says: "libuv, a C library that holds the event loop". The drawn station "V8 · event loop" and the <desc> teach the opposite of Chapter 12.
fix: Drawn station: "LOOP | browser event loop | Ch 12" and the next one "JS | V8 builds the request | Ch 12". In the <desc>: "the browser's event loop picks it up (12), and JavaScript, run by V8, builds the request (12)".
reason: Low severity but a plain factual slip in a drawn label. V8 runs the JavaScript; the event loop belongs to the embedder (the browser's renderer in Chrome, libuv in Node). The book's own Fig 12.6 draws the loop in libuv beside V8, and ch12-loop-p2 says the browser does the render step. The station 'V8 | event loop' contradicts Ch12.
judge_fix: Drawn stations: 'LOOP | browser event loop | Ch 12' then 'JS | V8 builds the request | Ch 12' (keep the Ch 12 credit). <desc>: 'the browser's event loop picks it up (12), and JavaScript, run by V8, builds the request (12)'. Words-drawn list changes to match.

quote: pods, orchestrated ... results ranked: cores, GPUs
problem: The Google stations name open-source and generic stand-ins for Google's real machinery. Google Search runs on Borg, which Chapter 17 calls Kubernetes' ancestor. Borg's unit is the task or alloc, not the Kubernetes pod. Google serves its search ranking models on its own TPUs, not GPUs: "for the first time we're using the latest Cloud TPUs to serve search results" (Google blog, "Understanding searches better than ever before", Oct 2019). Likewise, p3's boundary "HTTP query → SQL parser" names a SQL parser, and a search-index lookup has none.
fix: Drawn "pods, orchestrated" becomes "containers, orchestrated" (desc: "orchestrated containers (17)"). "results ranked: cores, GPUs" becomes "results ranked: cores, accelerators" (desc: "ranking on many cores and accelerators (16)"). In p3, "HTTP query → SQL parser" becomes "search query → index service".
reason: Partly. 'GPUs' for Google's ranking and 'pods' for Google's orchestration are stand-ins that a careful reader may flag (Google ranks on its own TPUs; its orchestrator is Borg, Ch17's own 'ancestor'). The SQL parser point is the clearest: a search-index lookup has no SQL parser, and 'into the database' in the desc names one. Generic wording is true everywhere and costs nothing. Borg-versus-pod alone would be taste, so keep the repair minimal.
judge_fix: Drawn 'pods, orchestrated' becomes 'containers, orchestrated' (desc: 'orchestrated containers (17)'). Drawn 'results ranked: cores, GPUs' becomes 'results ranked: cores, accelerators' (desc: 'ranking on many cores and accelerators (16)'). p3: 'HTTP query → SQL parser' becomes 'search query → query parser'. Desc: 'into the database' becomes 'into the index'.

quote: RSA will retire when error-corrected quantum computers (the logical qubits of Chapter 14) can run Shor's algorithm at scale
problem: RSA is being retired before such machines exist, because of harvest now, decrypt later. Chapter 14's Fig 14.13 strip teaches this, and this section's own Fig 18.3 strip says public keys "are moving to post-quantum algorithms now". NIST IR 8547 (initial public draft, Nov 2024) deprecates RSA and elliptic-curve keys after 2030 and disallows them after 2035. As written, the sentence suggests RSA stays until the quantum machine arrives.
fix: "RSA is already being retired, ahead of the error-corrected quantum computers (the logical qubits of Chapter 14) that could run Shor's algorithm at scale, and particular libraries will become archaic."
reason: The sentence says RSA retires when error-corrected quantum machines can run Shor's algorithm. The book elsewhere says the opposite order: Fig 18.3 strip 'public keys are moving to post-quantum algorithms now', and Ch14 (part-4 line ~2365) 'Harvest now, decrypt later ... which is why key exchange moved first'. The sentence also sits beside Fig 18.3, which puts RSA under 'fades'. NIST IR 8547 draft (Nov 2024) deprecates RSA/ECC after 2030 and disallows them after 2035. The reader will see a contradiction between the p3 sentence and the figure just above it.
judge_fix: 'x86 will eventually be a curiosity, RSA is already being retired, ahead of the error-corrected quantum computers (the logical qubits of Chapter 14) that could run Shor's algorithm at scale, and particular libraries will become archaic.' Source: NIST IR 8547 ipd (2024); Ch14 harvest-now strip.

quote: Modern economics is computational: markets are distributed systems, financial contracts are state machines, trading is a latency competition.

The paragraph then admits it ("These are slogans, but..."). The figure, caption and strip cover the same fields again, and biology appears three times.
